In the accomplishment by means of desire.
Liberation occurs through the path of existence, and both existence and non-existence bestow liberation.
The half-measure is the Lord of the Yoni (Bhageśvara), who is both with support and without support.
Having covered the face with a blue cloth, one should cause [the disciple] to enter.
Then, he should cause flowers to be scattered by him.
Or else, facing the east; and when there is no [other] possibility, one should [perform it] with one [verse], even though there are many [verses].
p. 19b) Now, the vidyā of the pledge (samaya-vidyā).

Oṃ, homage to Cāmuṇḍā, the fierce one, the shrieker! Duhi 2 phaṭ! To Jālandharī, whose conduct is that of Mahālakṣmī; to Vārāhī, who dwells in the cemetery of Nagala; to Karṇakubjā, the great-eared one; to the eight Mothers: Māheśvarī, Brahmāṇī, Vaiṣṇavī, Indrāṇī, Kaumārī, and Vārāhī!

Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍā, Mahālakṣmī, Śrīsiddhilakṣmībhairavī, Guhyaśrīmahākālī; O Māyā, O Mahāmāyā, grant all accomplishments! O Goddess who carries one across the entire cycle of existence, dweller in Koṭakāmarūpa, lover of the Bhairava of the cremation ground, fond of the practice of non-dual equanimity—Hrīṃ!
Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Aiṃ phreṃ huṃ hrīṃ cuṃ strīṃ śrīṃ kici 2 kili 2 hana 2 daha 2 grasa 2 he 2 hreṃ!

O Siddhibhairavī, who brings about the state of equal flavor for all yoginīs; you who dwell in the three worlds, who reside everywhere in forests, mountains, and difficult terrains, and who abide in the midst of battle—grant victory, grant total victory! Prade!
In the first [chapter], it is as follows: O you who dwell in the fast, O you who dwell upon the tree, O all-pervading one, O victory over all, O victorious one, O unconquered, O unvanquished!

Śrīṃ strīṃ staraṇī pūriṇī hrīṃ! Homage to the one of equal time, the one arisen from the two, the one who enters! Khphreṃ khreṃ śrīṃ strīṃ vūṃ phreṃ! Homage! Svāhā! This is the pledge-mantra (samaya-vidyā) of all yoginīs.
HŪṂ ||
*Bhairavasahitatrailokyamāte hreṃ ceṃ cheṃ namaḥ svāhā*. This is the *samaya-vidyā* of all the *yoginīs*.

This is the *vidyā* of all the Bhairavas and Bhairavīs, of all the *siddhis*, of all the *śākinīs*, and of all the *samayas*. By the recitation of this, one is honored everywhere— in all the *kṣetras* and *upapīṭhas* of all the *yoginīs*, all the gods, the *vidyādharas* and others, the *yakṣas* and others, and all the [protective] clans.
He becomes so; he protects himself everywhere; everywhere bound, he becomes liberated from all evil.

At the conclusion of the worship characterized by the lolling of the tongue, the *phetkāra* sounds, and the cries of "da da" and "hā hā," during the time of the commitment (*samaya*) with the goddesses, one should cause the mind to revolve for a long time within the mind at the source of manifestation. One should perform the recitation (*jāpa*) throughout the three junctions of the day while the head is joyful and nourished in every respect. In the abode of the deity, one should mentally utter "HŪM PHREṂ. By this, she becomes pleased; such is the rule for this commitment.
He desires knowledge; he performs that [rite].

Having first consecrated the mantra of the Goddess with the great conch-sutra and rosary, one should recite it at the three junctions of the day; success in the recitation is achieved after twenty-eight repetitions.
All mantras are accomplished. By making a garment from cloth burnt in a cremation ground and reciting [the mantra] over it, she appears before one's eyes.

If one is angry, she causes [the target] to fall. Having offered [the garment] to the Goddess, great liberation occurs through that. Having consecrated water with the mantra, she withdraws [the power]; by that, the person whom one desires to lead away is cast down. [This is done] with charcoal from a cremation ground.

By reciting [the mantra] one hundred times, he strikes whomsoever [he intends]. Having recited it over ashes from a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*) seven times, he should strike; they all become motionless like the dead. By that which is practiced as desired, if he strikes with charcoal from a cremation ground after reciting it one hundred times, they become unconscious. Having recited it over ashes from a cremation ground seven times...
He shall slay them; they all become motionless as if dead. One should sprinkle [the victim] with the Heart-mantra of the Goddess, and he becomes well-disposed.

Just as Bhairava does, so does she act. With the left [hand] one performs all rites; with the right... This Blessed Lady bestows success and assumes whatever form is desired. And one shall himself become Mahābhairava.

Like one beyond old age and death, he becomes free from old age and death; liberated from all diseases and devoid of all defects, he consumes all enemies like fire; and he asks what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.

Having consecrated a sword, sandals, or a pill, one attains accomplishment. One achieves the eight great accomplishments, such as various elixirs and rasāyana, as well as many kinds of minor accomplishments. Such a person cannot be slain by anyone.
With a mind constantly intent on recitation and bowing, he desires that and accomplishes it; the fever of those who live by others' livelihoods he destroys.

One causes an enemy to be seized by fever. And with the mere *sāman* chant, one seizes everyone. What need is there for much? What need is there for much? There is the accomplishment of the command (*ājñāsiddhi*). Whether it be the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), the mother-mantra (*mātṛkā*), the all-accomplishing mantra, or all mantras, they perform all tasks. When his accomplishment occurs in the cremation ground, it is accomplished through the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*).

The three worlds are accomplished. *Phe* & *valindadet*. One obtains the knowledge of Bhairava, which is difficult even for the thirty gods to attain. By this mere knowledge, one becomes a creator of dissolution and emanation within the very presence of the deities. This mantra should always be recited by the lords of yoga, whether standing, eating, drinking, or even during sexual union.

One should not abandon mental recitation (*mānasajāpa*). Having seen that, all people become deluded; she becomes one who deludes the world. One should always recite at night; [the mantras] then become embodied. One should always perform the worship of virgins according to the power of one's means. Then, if a woman desires accomplishment (*siddhi*), the accomplishment of the *yoginīs* comes to pass.
It stops the clouds; it causes explosions; and by its command, it makes even a god conform to the Dharma.
He wards off the sun; the accomplishment of sinlessness occurs. That yogin is Bhairava himself.

O Goddess, he will certainly attain success, for Bhairava is ever-present; otherwise, one does not attain success even by the God at any time. This king of the lords of mantras, the leader of the *pretas*, will cause [them] to reach [the goal].
O Viḍaṃvakas, the son of the Goddess is none other than you;

for as the Goddess accepts [the offering], she is attained through the destruction of deceit. For a man, death is inevitable within a thousand years; yet even one who is unmanifest, having bowed to the Supreme, the Transcendent, the Formless One—the highest secret of the Goddess—is perfected through purity by means of the mouth.
The procedure for the utterance of the mantra is Bhairava, O highly fortunate ones; Hrīṃ, Chchrīṃ, and Cūṃ are the heart of the Goddess, each one belonging to Maheśvarī.
Oṃ, homage to Bhairavī; first is the goddess, and the second is Kṣobhiṇī.
And the third vital point (marman) is indeed that which causes the great dissolution.
One should write the word *marmābhighāta* as the fourth word;
then the fifth is *kili kili*, followed by the words *tyava kici kici*; then *hrīṃ chrīṃ amukaṃ kāryam eva kuru 2 svāhā*.

Oṃ, homage! Hrīṃ khphreṃ hūṃ phreṃ! O Bhairavī, the agitator, the cause of the great dissolution! Strike at my vital points, strike at my vital points! Kili 2 kici 2! Hrīṃ chrīṃ! Accomplish such-and-such a task, accomplish it! Svāhā!

Thus addressed, [he said: "By this, that which is difficult even for the deities of mantra to obtain is accomplished; the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, are brought under control.

Having recited the Vidyā three times daily at the junctions of the day (*saṃdhyā*), performing ten thousand recitations, and having undertaken the great and supreme vow (*mahāsamaya*) while being devoted to the worship of the Guru, success (*siddhi*) arises through that. Then, that which was previously indicated..."
She performs her task; when uttered but once, she brings the entire world under her control. She accomplishes everything previously mentioned:
*phreṃ huṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
It is heard that even those [mantras] not explicitly mentioned are abandoned; when one is angry, they accomplish the recitation, and whatever one desires, that he performs.
During the burning fever, it causes agitation with piercing pain; then, seizing the heart, feet, and sight, it takes possession of the house.
Desiring that which has not departed from the mind, he performs it; he gathers it by means of its nature and bestows it.
He makes it two-edged.
By her will, she is perfected within the Blessed One as Advaitabhairavī, who has gone beyond the three cities.
She performs all rites and moves about at will, remaining present in the mind; having heard the mantras of those who follow Bhairava and are firm in their vows.
Likewise, this command of Bhairava must not be given to others; [only then] may one wander through the three worlds and always fill the realms.
Now I shall further proclaim another auspicious [practice] that bestows constant success;
by its shadow, the terrifying Jñānabhairava is set in motion. When the mind is to be withdrawn, one who is not black and is devoid of worldly attachment is beheld.
Having eaten from a leaf-cup or even remaining with others, one should not stand [thus]. Thus it has been told to you;
having understood this, when the substance is in hand and success is achieved, then the Raktani-sahacara and especially the Gṛdhraśiras [are employed].
One should apply auspicious collyrium, endowed with knowledge, to both eyes for the sake of all.
Intermingled with the left eye, he enters the seven netherworlds and assumes whatever form he desires.

The Supreme Lord; or else, in the *gulikā*. (p. 24b) "O Thou who art difficult to attain, the union of the *saṃrava* [mantra] is delightful. By the mere contemplation of this, it bestows omniscience. Because it is the cause and means for attaining success through the body of the Goddess, characterized by those [signs], the Supreme Goddess, known as the Seed (*bīja*), remains both hidden and unhidden.
The Śirīra-yoga is the most excellent. Whether it be one [deity] or all [of them], then what is the use of salutation?
One should not perform salutation toward that which is unaccomplished; indeed, one should abandon such [an object].
Oṃ phreṃ hūṃ Guhyakālī hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ.
Khphreṃ! O destroyer of all harmful afflictions through the application of tantras and mantras, *hara* 2 *hūṃ phaṭ*!
O you who possess the form of the Seer, *phreṃ phaṭ namaḥ svāhā*!
One should recite the mantra of *Pratyaṅgirā Siddhimukhī* three times. It subdues mechanical devices and drives away malevolent spirits.

In calamity, distress, the fear of the destruction of enemies, or in battle, success is attained through its recollection. Nothing whatsoever can prevail against that practitioner who is a great lord (*maheśvara*). Having performed a sprinkling with this [mantra], one may consume food and drink.
One should not be afraid; likewise, having offered flowers and incense, one should perform meditation and recitation.
The *adhikārapūjā* is performed on the eighth and fourteenth days, but not on any day when the daily worship (*nityapūjā*) is omitted.

On the eighth, ninth, fourteenth, the solar transits (saṃkrānti), the full moon, the new moon, and on Tuesdays, great accomplishment (mahāsiddhi) occurs through the worship of the additional lunar days (adhikaparva). Fever, planetary afflictions, and misfortunes are destroyed by the mere remembrance [of this].
The illustrious Bhairava said:

Having performed the great ritual commitment (mahāsamaya) directed toward this, one should recite it: "This supreme knowledge of Kālikā is dearer to her than life itself. This must be kept secret by those intent on all accomplishments (siddhi)."
Then it is said that the Supreme Goddess [reveals] the distinction and particularity of the divisions of karma.
By the mere knowledge of yoga, one becomes the destroyer of the thirty [gods].
The head [is located] at the two breasts, the two armpits, and the two shoulders; the two hands and feet at the two eyebrows;
the nose-tip at the abode of Nāka; and the throat and the abdomen; the navel and the big toes; the roots at both sides;
the crown of the head and the back at the two *vairoca*s; the *ṭeṭīka* and the root of the tongue; and the *rantala* at the root of the fingers.
From the head of Puṣpadanta onwards, Śiva dwells in these vital points (marmapradeśa) one by one; therefore, one should touch them.

O God, he who moves through the supreme vital points (marmas) always resides in the penis, the belly, the anus, all the joints, the navel, the neck, the temples, the heart, and the ears; he constantly wanders through the vital points of the ears,
the neck, the shoulders, and the cheeks.
Aiṃ draṃṣṭākalāli aiṃ hūṃ phreṃ marmamarmābhi phreṃ hana 2 hanaḥ 4 hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.

From the reduction of all impurities, by what does gold arise? It is through the piercing of the vital points (*marmābhipāta*). One should recite the mantra at the three junctions of the day (*trisandhyā*) with an extent of sixteen finger-breadths (*ṣoḍaśāṅgula*). One should protect the substance from all sides according to the sequence of the mantras of the upward-born (*ūrdhvaprajā*). With the fingers, [one should perform the rite] for two finger-breadths.

In four stages: the substance consists of half a finger-breadth, a leaf, and a *pala*. [There are] those who are delighted and satisfied with gold, and those with abundant, excellent nectar. There are not five *palas* on the fingers; there are five *palas* by means of successive halving. Twelve by two is the sequence; they are exceedingly swift, fragmented, and without limbs.
Having multiplied the substance by the finger-measure, one should divide it by the part;

having made the finger-measure into finger-units, one should divide it by one's own hand. The remaining substance is likewise [treated] by the specific calculation of Śiva’s two eyes (two), the vulture and cat eyes (four), and the owl-head (one)—[that is, by fifteen]. (p. 27b) [The result is] burnt.
One should cultivate [the realization] within all ointments.
One should anoint the pair of eyes with Narataila, well-consecrated by the recitation of the heart-mantra.

Merely by applying this ointment, one becomes invisible; one beholds the Gālikās and the measure and number of substances. This is the sacrifice of accomplishment (*siddhi-yāga*); through mere desire, everything comes to pass.
The yoga of meditative concentration.
For killing, it is black in form; for subjugation, it is proclaimed to be red;
for driving away, it is smoke-colored; and for pacification, it is proclaimed to be white.
In the rite of paralyzing, Maheśvarī is yellow in color and possesses a form according to her will; this is the supreme secret and the very determination of reality.
Oṃ phreṃ siddhi kalāli hrīṃ cchrīṃ hūṃ strīṃ phreṃ namaḥ svāhā.
This is that supreme goddess who should always be recited by the wise.

All rites are accomplished; indeed, one may accomplish them simply by contemplating them with the mind. How much more so, then, does the Mistress of Yogins (*yogīśvarī*) grant accomplishment through the secret yoga of contemplation! She brings about the assembly of yoginīs (*yoginīmelāpa*), she reveals all auspicious dreams, and the gathering of yoginīs (*yoginīmelaka*) arises spontaneously of its own accord.

By this, one performs all actions. The accomplishment of one's desires occurs through the mind and speech. By uttering various forms of sound, one attains the state of the goal of accomplishment (siddhi). One brings about a gathering of yoginīs;
one beholds auspicious dreams and perceives the form of Śiva. At that time, all the goddesses and yoginīs [appear].
Having offered a blood oblation with the secret heart-mantra and having prepared the central mandala, one should draw [the image] for the Bhairava-yogin.

Never by any other means. The maiden should be made to focus her attention. She should be drawn in the secret place with wine as the ink. Having offered a bali-oblation with the supreme secret heart-mantra, one should purify it with the five nectars using the heart-mantra ending in the syllable *hrīḥ*. Then, having approached all the substances such as wine and so forth, one performs the summoning.
It cuts through the mantras of others. It becomes a means of shattering those mantras once it has been accomplished.
By means of this mantra, one should cause the offices to be granted; having granted the offices to one's own disciple.
He should cause [them] to recite; he reads.
Sakula did not see hell because of Vimalaka; by means of recitation in the heart, he saw all beings.
One does whatever one desires. One should cause the mental disposition of the Guru to arise, for that is the cause of all accomplishments (*siddhi*);

therein he shall become the Lord of the Tantra. This refers primarily to the Tantras of the Yoginīs. *Kuru ḍi ḍāṃ kṣo*, O Śivā, this supreme secret has been given by me; let the Goddess behold its merit.
No other fortune exists besides this; wherever Bhairava is established, by remembering him even once, he brings it about.
By her will, Yāginī Bhairavī is Guhyakālī, the essence of all principles (*sarvatattva*), who has transcended the five principles (*pañcatattva*).

By means of the collyrium of the support (*ādhārāñjana*) of that path of yoga, she causes the water to whirl like a house. Having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, one becomes a yogi; such a yogi is himself Bhairava. Within the pores of his skin are more than eighty million Bhairavas.

[The mantras] are thus established. Alternatively, Bhairavī should be recited eight thousand times; indeed, she alone should be recited while meditating on her as red. In this way, great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*) comes to the practitioner through speech. By writing [this] and at the commencement of its recitation, no living being is harmed.
And the writing, O Goddess, should not be done with wine or red lac;
it should be with the seed-syllable of Bhairava and indeed with the blood of Carcikā.
One should not begin the yoga practice at the junction of the two *māyā* seed-syllables.
Whether alone or even in a secluded place, for one who recites while holding a conch shell and a rosary consecrated with liquor,
the name of Bhairava is said to be proclaimed in its entirety.
On the new moon day,
or on the eighth or fourteenth lunar days, one should diligently worship the sacred book and perform the supreme recitation of mantras.
Likewise, it should be diligently constructed by these two within a monastery.
May the playful manifestation of the yogi who is eternally established in the state of non-dual conduct be present.
Then, having put on a pair of blue cloths, with disheveled hair and red unguents, one should perform recitation (*japa*) out of the joy of wine.
Endowed with power (*śakti*), through the practice of non-duality (*advaitācāra*), one becomes Bhairava in person.

Then, by the recitation of the seventeenth [verse], one shall become Bhairava before long. By the recitation of the sixteen-syllable mantra, through three preliminary practices (*puraścaraṇa*), one attains perfection at night; with a body enveloped in supreme power and by moving within the innermost [space], one may uphold all scriptures and the like. Merely by remembering it, no one whatsoever shall stand before him in battle.

Having thrown tiger, bear, and jackal skins, along with *veṣṭikana*, *śiva*, *huṃ*, and flowers, into the doorway of another’s house, one makes [the inhabitants] assume the form of animals. One should grind the flesh of a jackal and a cat with the blood of a dog; reciting this together, one steals the enemy's property and everything from the other’s house.

He sees [them]. He becomes invisible. Alternatively, if one applies a pill placed in the mouth with a paste of *sivarasa*, *cchāgarasa*, and the milk of a tawny (*kapilā*) goat ground together, it paralyzes fire.

Having placed a pill dyed with cat-blood into the mouth of a woman in her fertile period, and having moistened it with the blood of a white *māṇḍaka* mixed with the blood of a *caṇḍāla*, she should wash her eyes in water mixed with the blood of a female jackal.

It becomes invisible. Whatever one draws with her blood, that she brings about. By means of a portion of her, together with [her] half, one becomes inexhaustible. Having bound [the materials] with liquor, blood, and so forth, using a cemetery thread, one should smear [the image] with the hand;
by means of white, yellow, or red [pigments], she becomes possessed of various forms.

The powder of a skull should be applied to the head; one becomes deformed. These are the supreme among the supreme, bestowing success; they are the practice for constant accomplishment, O Bhairavī. They must be kept secret.
No other mantra among thousands of mantras can surpass them, as declared by the Radiant One. They were fashioned by the Supreme Excellence to grant success.
The illustrious Bhairava said:

Listen, O Bhairavī, Goddess of the Gods, to this [teaching] which destroys all sins. For the sake of destroying the sins of the world, you have placed it in your heart. This scripture was brought from the presence of Guru Bhairava, or even composed by yourself for the purpose of [piercing] the tip of the iron arrow (nārāca). It consists of one, two, four, five, six— (Note: The text appears to be fragmentary; the final line likely refers to the number of syllables in the mantra.)

Those who are devoted to the seven-syllable [mantra] and others, though possessing sin, do not know [this]; yet when recited, they desire accomplishment, and the eight great siddhis are said to be attained even in an instant.
Those joined with a mass of evil do not attain success.

The Great Goddess of the Mālā-mantra bestows the fruit of swift accomplishment. Through practice, O Great Goddess, even over hundreds of millions of births, those who lack the practice of the hundred repetitions do not achieve success with the Single Syllable.
By that, O Goddess of the Gods, one who is attaining perfection shall become Bhairava himself.
The accomplishment of the single-syllable mantra occurs at all times through seven hundred thousand recitations.
The five-syllable mantra [is mastered] by sixteen lakhs, and the nine-syllable [mantra] by nine lakhs.
There are sixteen syllables multiplied by seven hundred thousand.
It consists of seventeen syllables; with six hundred thousand [repetitions], it becomes one of twenty syllables.
It consists of forty-four syllables and has exactly one hundred thousand [repetitions].
From nine syllables, there are four hundred thousand [mantras].
The hundred-syllable mantra and the three-syllable mantra are to be recited.
By two hundred thousand [recitations] of the five-hundred-syllable [mantra].
The great garland of one thousand syllables is perfected through one hundred thousand recitations; thus the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) becomes accomplished.

Having performed [the rite] four times the number prescribed for the Age of Brahma-conduct (Brahmacarya-yuga), it must be performed fourfold in the Kali age; having become equipped with power at night, gladdened by the joy of wine, and with hair disheveled, one should perform the preliminary service (puraścaryā) according to the stated number, either with the five-fold [mantra] or by the left-hand path.

Success is attained. Those mantras consisting of one syllable, or two, three, four, five, six, seven, and so on, which are red in color, possess great splendor, have no beginning or end, and are pervasive—those who desire success through recitation shall obtain them; they attain the eight great siddhis.
As long as the mass of sins accumulated in previous births remains, so long will there be no success. Through the *puraścaraṇa* recitation, sins are destroyed and success is attained.
O Great Goddess, the Great Garland bestows swift success.
Through practice, O Great Goddess, [the fruit] attained over ten million births [is realized].

The single-syllable [mantras] do not succeed through a hundred repetitions; rather, O Goddess of Gods, they are mastered through the application of practice, whereby one becomes manifest and equal to Śiva. The garland-mantra (*mālāmantra*), O Great Goddess, bestows the fruit of swift accomplishment.
By the mere knowledge of this, the yogi becomes a destroyer of the gods;
having understood this with effort, Guhyacaṇḍī Maheśvarī— Kālī, who always bestows perfection— [is attained] through the grace of the guru’s feet.
Having completely renounced all books, all yogas, and all vows.
